en: The Lineage of the Hatthavanagalla Monastery.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
To her whose heart is overflowing with affection, who is like a jasmine flower free from stain—
May the Lamp of the Victor, ignited by the stage of wisdom,
forever illuminate the beautiful heap of meanings of the words, driving away all the darkness of my delusion.
Among the sovereigns consecrated in Laṅkā, there was a king named Sirisaṅghabodhi, who possessed the virtues of a Bodhisattva;
through the medium of composing his exceedingly beautiful life story, [this work is presented].
I shall relate the history of the Hatthavanagalla Monastery. It was established by the one of noble lineage,
the compassionate one whose mind is intent on the welfare of others,
renowned as the bearer of the yoke of sovereignty over all ascetics.
And how can I, perceiving "I am engaged in activity," exert myself in this manner based on what was previously written? 4.
In Laṅkā, where the stains of the poison of evil views have been washed away by the river of the nectar of the Sugata’s tradition, in the Great Nāga Grove Garden of the Blessed One Aṅgīrasa...

There is a district named Maṇibheda, which has become a place of perfected excellence for the world-conquering exploits of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas assembled in the *samiti* (councils), and which serves as an ornament to the island-land of Siṃhala;
it is distinguished by various mines of gems and possesses highly precious varieties of jewels.
Having obtained the Teacher’s choice, which cannot be attained by others—
Like a banner of victory raised high by the mountain-peak of Mount Sumanakūṭa, which delights in pride,
the river Śuddhoruvālukā adorns this place.
In the removal of the hosts of *yakkhas* from Laṅkā, the Victor experienced the heat caused by the contact of the leather seat, the needle, and the cloth;
[he also perceived] the bubbles of the foam of existence within the *rākṣasa* of *saṃsāra*.
There, on the great courtyard, stands the King of Stupas. It is for those who have gathered there to drink from the great river of the constant,
great flood that the water is provided.
The collection of the essence of the waters has surely gone to the form of a permanent stupa;
it is seen within the stainless water of that river.
The reflection of the moon, shimmering with waves,
shines as it is led away by its own coils— the serpent’s hoods—
encircling it with their bodies, like those seeking to offer worship.
9. In a village on the outskirts of that Mahiyaṅgaṇa Mahāvihāra, there lived a kṣatriya named Selābhaya.
Having obtained a son, he showed him to the readers of bodily marks. Those men, having examined the boy’s bodily marks, said:
"This prince is not one who possesses the nature of a commoner. He is endowed with the marks of grain and merit; even the entire..."
"Having made the island of Siṃhala a single umbrella [of sovereignty], he will display great and wonderful marvels and the deeds of a great hero," they prophesied. Then,
Prince Selābhaya, upon hearing of his son’s future prosperity beginning with the consecration, was overcome by an exceeding joy that reached its peak.
At that time, while ruling in the city of Anurādhapura, King Vohāratissa, fearing that some calamity might arise from him at any moment,

took the prince and laid him down in the midst of the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Great Elder Nanda, who had assembled for the recitation of protective charms (paritta) in the courtyard of the Bodhi tree at the Mahiyaṅgaṇa Mahāvihāra.
“Venerable sir, this boy goes for refuge to the Great Saṅgha and to the Great Bodhi Tree;
may all the venerable ones protect him, and let his name be Saṅghabodhi.
Having thus entrusted him to the Great Saṅgha and the deity of the Bodhi Tree, he passed away while tending to the boy when the boy was seven years old.
11. Then his maternal uncle, the Great Elder Nanda, brought the youth to the monastery and, while looking after him, had him master the entire word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Piṭakas;
he also made him reach the highest proficiency in the external sciences.

Because he had performed his duties and possessed sharp wisdom, Saṅghabodhi Kumāra became endowed with knowledge and consciousness, and upon reaching maturity, he was as pleasing to the eyes of the world as a lotus.
There arose a roar of praise for her excellence of form, which was being relished by all with palms joined in reverence, and for her perfection of virtuous conduct.

What more need be said?—From her mass of hair, dark blue and glossy like a cluster of *kadamba* flowers, she possessed the quality of a lovely, long, and supple strand; from her face, which surpassed the full orb of the moon, she possessed the quality of a charming, serene, and gentle radiance;
and from her excellent conch-shell neck, golden-hued, she possessed a richness, nobility, and gracefulness that was both profound and sublime.

In the parts of her neck, there was a compact grace arising from a beautiful accumulation of folds; on the surface of her chest, there was a form that was plump, long, and elegant like the branches of a celestial tree;
in her pair of arms, which were the very source for the granting of desires, there was a playful gait like that of an elephant in rut;

in her pair of legs, which were shaped like elephants' trunks, there was a beauty like that of a pair of golden mirrors shining with the splendor of a most excellent chariot, reaching down to the knees. Always...
The composition of this descriptive text brings great honor to his physical form— so exceedingly beautiful, noble, and graceful—
which was fashioned by the craft of the Perfections (pāramitā-dhamma-sippa) as he took from a lotus a pair of feet with tender red petals and joined them together.
His body was endowed with auspicious marks and filled with the bloom of fresh youth.
What description can there be for this golden form,
which possesses a radiance born from the gathering of praise,
and which wafts forth a transcendental fragrance on all sides?
Having conquered the city of the heart’s fortress,
the two enemies, he consecrated the King of Dharma there like a dear friend; then,
speaking these words of instruction for his benefit, he said:
There, the wise one set forth his own bodily conduct.
Thus ends the first chapter, "The Birth of the Prince.
15. Then, on one occasion, at the conclusion of a discourse on the Dhamma, the venerable uncle, the Great Elder, [addressed] the prince Sirisaṅghabodhi, who had reached maturity.
Having addressed him, he spoke thus: “O Prince! O you of great fortune! Now you have mastered the scriptures of the Sugata and are conversant with all external treatises.

You have reached the pinnacle of the fourfold types of wisdom; nevertheless, you are born into a Kshatriya clan whose wealth is pride, your body is adorned with youthfulness that pervades the entire earth, and your beauty is peerless and superhuman.”
"And as for strength"—there is a great and powerful succession of all forms of misconduct; not even a single one of their bases is insignificant, so what need be said of their combination?
"For the most part, though the intellect may become stainless by being washed away by the waters of the Teacher's doctrine, it nevertheless falls into turbidity;
and though the view of those arrogant with fresh youth has not abandoned its whiteness, it becomes truly full of passion. It carries away...

And like a withered leaf in a whirlwind, nature carries a man far away from himself by means of his own desires during the time of youth. Bearing the burden of the senses, seeking the deer of sensual enjoyment through the most difficult of paths,
this is precisely the time for you to find satisfaction in the taste of the object of the teacher’s instruction, while you are still not yet worn out by the power of the arrows of passion.
In the hearts of the wise, it melts like water; base nature, devoid of cause, does not burn—neither lineage nor learning can withstand the heat of a mind’s malice.
Is fire not hot by its very nature? Or does the submarine fire become any less fierce because of the water? Therefore, you must be instructed with even greater firmness.
16. For when the mind is free from stain, the qualities of the instruction enter it like the rays of the moon entering a cat's-eye gem;
the word of the teacher, though stainless, produces a great expansion of knowledge like water striking a vast expanse, whereas for one incapable of realization, it is like a stake struck by hearing.
But for one capable, it brings forth a far greater abundance of honor, beauty, and splendor, like all ornaments upon an elephant, [a state] established from time immemorial.
For a mind that follows the currents of craving, defilements, and the sense-faculties does not lead to its own welfare;

therefore, O King, through the power of mindfulness, both princes and ascetics achieve victory over the sense-faculties, which produces a multitude of wholesome states pertaining to both the present life and the future.
And this victory over the sense-faculties arises from attending upon teachers and elders, practicing their instructions without transgression.
Therefore, until the end of life, one must not abandon devotion to the three refuges as one's primary goal.
One must not perform that which awakens the epilepsy of passion nor that which serves as water for extinguishing the fire of sense objects;
rather, let him behold with the eye of virtuous resolve the moth, enslaved by its craving for the eye-faculty, falling into the blazing flame of a lamp. Let him likewise behold the ear-faculty...
For one devoted to pleasure, it is like a young deer facing an arrow’s flight; for a bee under the sway of its sense of smell, it is like being struck by the palm of an elephant in rut;
for a cat addicted to the gratification of its sense of taste, it is like falling into a snare of bait;
and for an elephant longing to experience its sense of touch, it is like meeting with captivity in the water.

When these faculties are joined together, how can we describe the vast web of suffering to be reached by one who desires through the service of the five objects of sense-pleasure? Let the discerning person reflect constantly upon these well-spoken words.
The wise man looks forward to some small pleasure of the household life,
knowing it is merely for the sake of maintaining the body;
even when associating with a young woman, he remains unmoved by the delusion of passion.
The conceit of pleasure in a forest is like the scratching of an itch.
What man would serve another, or endure humiliation,
if that were not a bond of suffering, like a shackle upon one's wife?
The tuft of hair on the forehead,
though constantly drawn toward the face, always turns away from it;
even when reaching far, it leaves behind its own quality.
Such sloth indeed causes even a man who has never been intimate with her to enter within,
just as a wall [allows entry] through the very act of being built.
Like a vine with its tendrils,
women are to be guarded by the hands in all their parts;
like a reed, they are empty within and without when held inside and lacking support outside.
They bring about his very destruction; one should place no trust in those who are mothers of anger.
For one whose mind is steeped in evil, the various hells stand wide open on all sides like wicked friends; there is no liberation from the state of universal fear.

Moreover, the serpent of anger, coiled within the hollow of the tree-trunk of the heart, must never be released outside. Rather, by one who possesses the power of patience, it should be drawn back even as it does not flick its hood.
For those who are shrouded in the armor of patience, the birds of harsh speech belonging to the wicked may remain [without harming them].
These flowers of praise for the assembly bloom upon that garland of virtues;
[so too do] sovereignty over the world and abundant wealth.
Even having obtained a son and a wife who are agreeable to one's mind,
craving never ceases its wandering;
do not let craving cause you distress.
Though one’s physical beauty and radiance are pleasant,
if wealth and livelihood decline, beings will overcome that person as if they were enemies.
May that [thought] leave your heart.
Weariness and repulsion toward misfortunes do not [lead to liberation];
therefore, one should not resort to a dejected state of mind.
They say that energy accompanied by wisdom is for the sake of grasping success in all matters.
The activities of all beings are undertaken for the purpose of happiness.
"And happiness does not exist apart from the Dhamma; therefore, be devoted to the Dhamma.

When the Great Elders were thus teaching the path of the conduct of the virtuous, he—due to that unwholesome state—either through a face distorted by a frown born of disrespect and unwillingness to listen, or with eyes cast toward the horizon, or by closing his eyes like an elephant in the grip of self-conceit, [acted] under the sway of egoism.

As if casting aside his own wisdom, with his soft hands joined in a *añjali* placed low, with his head bowed down and inclined toward him, and with a face whose cheeks blossomed with shouts of "Well done! born of rapture;
with a body covered by a mantle of bristling hair standing on end across all its limbs, he prostrated himself upon the ground as if having attained the long-sought-for fruit of the Path.
He manifested a state of even greater joy.
Thus ends the second chapter, the Chapter on Instruction.

30. From that time forth, without transgressing the aforementioned practice and content with his own spiritual restraint, the Elder Mahā Mātula—desiring to preserve the name Saṅghabodhi for him—began to use the designation "Dhammika."
31. Believing the words of the readers of marks, he did not allow his nephew—who desired to go forth—to do so, saying:
"For this prince, living here in Anurādhapura rather than elsewhere will bring about security from bondage;
it is a place where the ripening of merit arises in accordance with one's deeds, and by performing the duties and services for the Mahācetiya, a great mass of merit will be accumulated."
Thinking, “He will succeed,” the Elder took the prince and set out, desiring to go to Anurādhapura.

Saṅghatissa, Goṭhābhaya, and two other long-eared princes—having been companions of the prince since their childhood play—also set out together with him. Taking those three princes, the Elder departed.
He entered Anurādhapura even earlier. Among those princes who were following the Great Elder, the eldest was Saṅghatissa, the middle one Saṅghabodhi, and the youngest Goṭhābhaya;
these three, following behind the Elder, proceeded in succession by way of the Setumattha bridge across the Tissavāpī tank.
32. There, while sitting in the Setusālā, a certain blind seer heard the sound of the footsteps of those three princes as they were crossing over.
Examining them according to their physical marks, he prophesied to those sitting there: "These three shall all become sovereigns of the land in the island of Siṃhala.
Later, Goṭhābhaya, traveling along, heard that speech and [the words] of the others...
Without informing those who were traveling with him, he returned and asked, "Which one will rule the kingdom for a long time?
Is he establishing a firm foundation? When it was told to him that it was the younger one, he became exceedingly joyful and overjoyed;
returning even more swiftly, he went along with them and, because of his sharp intelligence and profound nature, without letting anyone know, [entered] the inner palace.
He entered. They all three took up residence in suitable dwellings.
Then the youngest brother, thinking, "These two, though established in the kingdom, will not live long because they are short-lived;
I alone shall rule their kingdom," and thus aspiring to obtain the kingdom for himself by a corresponding means, [acted].
Showing the means, [the elder said], "Frequently intoxicated. Even the elder, being exceedingly fond of him, practiced exactly what he was instructed;
and seeing this, the king granted him honor and, becoming the leader in all royal affairs, he soon became a favorite of the king.
At that time, a kshatriya named King Vijaya, who was ruling the kingdom, was well-disposed toward him.
Making him alone the foremost in all royal affairs, he appointed him as the commander-in-chief.
However, because Dhammika had no desire for kingship, he did not even give rise to a thought of seeking the throne;
rather, acting solely by the instruction of the Great Elder, he would merely attend upon the king at the time of his audience and follow him to the royal palace.
Having entered and then departed from there with them, he remained that evening in the Great Elder’s monastery itself;
without neglecting his own righteous duties and practicing blameless Dhamma such as attending upon the Mahācetiya during its construction and while it was under repair, he passed his time.

At that time, Saṅghatissa, having brought the entire kingdom and the city into his own hands, found an opportunity one day to have King Goṭhābhaya killed within the palace itself and established himself in the kingship.
Thus ends the third chapter, the Entry into Anurādhapura.
35. Then Goṭhābhaya, having appointed Dhammika to the position of general even though he was unwilling, became himself the treasurer, looking toward the future.
Then King Saṅghatissa, while producing much merit and demerit, [reigned] at the time when the rose-apple fruit ripens.
Accompanied by his army, his ministers, and his harem, he went frequently to the eastern region and ate the jambu fruits.
Because of the king’s constant coming and going, the inhabitants of the kingdom, being greatly distressed, mixed poison into the jambu fruits that were fit for the king’s consumption.
Then King Saṅghatissa passed away right there from that poison.
36. Then Goṭhābhaya, recollecting the words of Andhavicakkhaṇa, gradually had the kingdom bestowed [upon Saṅghabodhi].
Later, thinking, "I shall become well-established," he, together with his ministers and his army, invited Prince Saṅghabodhi to the kingship.
He, however, because of the dangers seen by the Great Bodhisatta Temiya, did not experience the relinquishing of the pleasures of kingship.
Even though he was entreated again and again, remembering the great web of suffering, Abhaya continued to refuse.
He gathered all the people from the villages, market towns, and royal capitals, and although he entreated them in various ways along with them, he was unable to make them accept [the proposal].
Then all the inhabitants of the kingdom and the ministers went to the Mahāvihāra and assembled the Great Saṅgha.
In the midst of the Saṅgha, the youth Saṅghabodhi, having prostrated before the great Saṅgha while lying upon the ground, was granted leave;
sitting to one side, he began to speak thus:
"Indeed, this so-called royal glory, however much it shines, becomes only as soiled with lampblack as the flame of a camphor lamp."
Only the mass of karma rises up. For indeed, this stream of rain from the clouds of association is for the poisonous creepers of craving;

it is a sweet-sounding trap for the deer of the sense-faculties; it is a streak of smoke from the fire of misapprehension, a bed for the delusion of negligence, and the rising of darkness for the vision of wisdom;
it is the vanguard banner of the great army of indiscipline, and the source of rebirth.
The onset of anger is a crocodile; the drinking-place is the mouth of wrong view. The assembly hall is the cave-dwelling of the vices of power and theatrical displays;
the drum-roll is the thorny vine of the conduct of the wicked. The arrival of unseasonable rain is for the swans of good conduct;
the raising of the curtain is for the drama of hypocrisy. The plantain tree is the executioner’s noose for the stalk of virtue.
O Moon of Dhamma, you are like the mouth of Rāhu to the orb of the moon; for I see no one else who, even though unacquainted with her, has not been utterly overwhelmed by her, nor deceived.

Furthermore, just as the sprinkling of auspicious water from the ceremonial jars at the time of the consecration of princes serves to wash away impurity, so too does the skill of the priest lead to purification, yet the heart becomes stained by the smoke of the fire-oblation, just as the tip of a blade of kusa grass is blackened by its own cleansing.
Patience carries one away as if by a vehicle; the perception of the arrival of old age is covered as if by the binding of a turban-ribbon;
the longing for the next world is hidden as if by a sunshade; and the blows from the rattan canes of truth are fanned far away as if by the breeze of a yak-tail whisk.
Thus, some who are intoxicated by the wine of royal glory cast aside all virtues to a great distance.
They entertain themselves with messengers who are intent on accomplishing their own purposes, who are greedy for wealth, fame, and food, and who are like cranes among reeds;
they consider the pursuit of another's wife to be a sport, the exhaustion of hunting grounds to be a pastime, the drinking of liquor to be elegance, constant negligence to be a state of refinement,
the abandonment of one’s own wife to be freedom from calamity, and the disregard of the teacher’s word to be independence.
He thinks: "Dancing and singing are to be enjoyed for their pleasure; attachment to crowds and delight in aesthetic flavors are things he endures out of patience;
being a leader is his wisdom; the words of those who praise him are his fame; his restlessness is his enthusiasm.
Thus, by attributing even this collection of faults to the side of virtues, he himself—[remains] impartial and free from partiality.
Being deceived by internal, skillful seducers and rogues who flatter them with superhuman praises,
their minds intoxicated by pride, they falsely attribute to themselves qualities they do not possess; though they share the common human condition,
they imagine themselves to be divine, descended from heaven, and superhuman, while all people perceive them as such due to the power of their performed deeds which appear to be truly divine.
They assume a state of radiance. And they rejoice in their own body being sustained by the life-force of those who live in dependence upon it. 38.

They regard their own pair of arms—which have entered within [the chest] and been struck down by the honor arising from the deception of imposing the status of a celestial deity upon the mind—as if they were another pair of arms. Their entire forehead is covered by eyes veiled by skin.
Transmigrating from month to month, filled with the pride of false esteem, they do not honor the deities, they do not worship the ascetics and brahmins, nor do they revere those worthy of reverence;
they do not attend upon their teachers even when seeing them, being intent on what is harmful and indifferent to the sight of the venerable.
They mock the self-restrained, saying, "What pleasure is there in the enjoyment of sense-objects? They do not listen to the instruction of the elders, thinking, "Old age will destroy my existence."
“‘One’s own wisdom is despised’—thus the minister spoke of him as a mere needle;
‘He is like a rhinoceros’—referring to one who speaks only for absolute benefit—and by such words, he said: ‘I do not desire this sovereignty, which is a mine of many faults.
39. Then the Great Sangha, respectfully seated in their midst, turned toward the Prince and said: ‘O you of great fortune!’”
Just as leeches clinging to the breasts of a woman cause pain there with their sharp suckers and draw out only blood,
while the infant, producing a sense of comfort for his mother with his tender mouth, sucks only milk; even so,
the foolish and undisciplined man who has attained royal power accumulates only much demerit, whereas the wise and disciplined person [accumulates merit].
However, having scrutinized with wisdom both the frailty of the life-force and the worthlessness of accumulated wealth, you fulfill the ten wholesome courses of action;
thus, by means of such a vast mass of riches, you accumulate a great heap of merit. You are one who has undertaken the burden of a Great Being through your resolve toward the Dhamma;
having obtained such a field for the production of merit, [you should act] in accordance with the Dhamma.

"Protecting the world with impartiality, upholding the teaching of the Sugata, and having brought the perfection of generosity to its ultimate limit, you should subsequently go forth into homelessness and bring the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) to full maturity.
Thus he instructed him. Then that supreme man of great aspiration, being unable to disregard the instruction of the Great Saṅgha, consented.

Immediately thereafter, the great multitude of people, with the consent of the Saṅgha, made the entire Island of Virtue a single umbrella, consecrated it, and established the title Dhammika Sirisaṅghabodhi Rājā;
they also appointed Goṭhābhaya to the position of commander-in-chief.
He gave alms, maintained the perpetual observance of the precepts, and practiced constant virtue.
He practiced patience and heedfulness;
with a benevolent disposition toward all beings and a gentle nature,
he shone forth as the very embodiment of the Dhamma.
Having understood the true nature of the world,
and having followed the practice of striving and the course of striving,
he desires to lay down the Dhamma among people.
He too was attached to the obstruction of these phenomena.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, "The Consecration of the Kingdom. 44.
That king, having caused a costly and vast distribution of voting tickets (*salākagga*) to be made in the Great Monastery (*Mahāvihāra*), [bestowed them] upon many thousands...
He established a regular system of voting tickets (*salāka*) for the monks' meals. Furthermore,
having had a large monastery and a private residence (*pariveṇa*) built in his own name for the Elder Mātula Mahāthera, he provided it with many articles of lawful use (*kappiyabhaṇḍa*),
and at the seventh watch of the night, while in seclusion, he caused the surrounding villages and fields to be designated as communal property (*saṅghika-paribhoga*) fit for the use of the community.
Observing the difficult deeds of the Great Bodhisattva, he resolved to accomplish such a heroic feat himself.
For it was said: "When suppliants cried out, 'Give me such-and-such a garment,' he could not say, 'I am unable,' nor 'I have nothing,' nor 'I will not give.'"
"Since the opportunity has been seized by Great Compassion within my mind, may craving go far away from me, as if it were traveling to a distant land.
And when will there be for me, like that of our Bodhisatta, the great festival of the renunciation of external objects? Thus he thought.
It is brought in by the striking of sharp weapons,
and driven out again and again with the effort of warding off the blows;
thus, it is exhausted by the force of this repeated coming and going.
"Alas, suffering did not afflict his heart.

Thus, at the time of giving his internal possessions—his flesh, blood, and so forth—the Great Being’s mind was not oppressed by painful sensations, nor did he think, "When will such a great auspicious occasion for the gift of my own internal possessions come to me?
Then that serpent Saṅkhapāla, overcome by the force of the poison, [fainted].
Unshaken by the fear of breaking his moral precepts,
yet desiring out of compassion to go himself— though he was without means— to those noble families who were wasting away their bodies and wealth, he surely grieved deeply.
Thinking, "When shall I attain the glory of the foundation of guarding virtue thus?
the fool might drink both milk and the deathless nectar;
yet once he has grown up, he will loathe that very same thing.
Having experienced sovereignty in this way, he will eventually, through the ripening of knowledge, constantly abandon it.
And [he thinks]: "In this manner, I too must certainly go forth into homelessness before long."
Thus Senaka recognized that snake, which was like a poison-pot for brahmins,
as something extraordinary due to his mind being defiled by hatred;
what need is there to mention him when his mind is free from hatred?
"By what means shall such an attainment of noble knowledge—
achieved through the ten perfections for the sake of omniscience— be accomplished by me? Thinking thus,
even when he was of the *kisakalaṇḍaka* breed and possessed only a tuft of hair, [he remained steadfast].
He strove to drain the waters of the ocean;
that would not have been due to a lack of intelligence,
for he possessed the capacity to accomplish whatever he desired.
Having thus practiced the perfection of energy, thinking, "When shall I become a worthy vessel?",
even though King Kalābu, unsatisfied,
had ordered his execution, the Teacher of Forbearance remained steadfast.
"May I purify my heart of hatred with patience;
may I understand the seizing of deceptive stratagems.
And when shall I adorn myself by thus fulfilling the perfection of a kshatriya?"
Even the sandals of the one named Rāma could not endure his wrongful assault;
for that hero spoke nothing other than the truth.
Thus he was a pillar of truth, a proclaimer of the Four Truths.
And he thought: "When shall I too, by such power of the perfection of truth, become capable of awakening the Four Truths for the entire world?
Thus was he known to Mugapakkha as one who feared the loss of his glory.
Having firmly resolved upon the rules of conduct beginning with the "Muka" vow,
I endured that very same kind of suffering, even though it was unbearable,
until I had gone forth and broken through [the world].
Thus, thinking, "When will the fulfillment of my own resolve-perfection (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramitā) come to pass?",
he experienced horripilation through the power of loving-kindness (mettā), making his hair stand on end as he was bound by affection.
Even toward those who were equal to him, the steadfast one harbored eternal enmity and made sounds of hostile intent. And he thought:
"When shall I too reach the pinnacle of such perfection in loving-kindness?"
Thus the Single King was known for his equanimity;
he was like a scale, impartial toward honor and dishonor;
having transcended both pleasure and anger, he cultivated equanimity.
In all circumstances, his mind was devoid of the fluctuations of rapture.
Thus, even while living as a householder, he constantly reflected: "When shall I become one who shares [the perfections] with all?
This concludes the fifth chapter, "The Aspiration for the Perfections."
56. While he was thus ruling the kingdom with a faultless dharma, once, due to the ripening of some unwholesome karma of his subjects—
[a being appeared] with a belly like a cooking pot, with crooked thighs and knees,
and a body as formidable as a water-laden cloud with a peaked roof.
With his staff-like fangs, crooked and hard, clenched together, he was a demon who devoured men for nine days.
He would sit at the outskirts of various villages, and whichever people approached him would wait for that night-eater.
Their eyes turn red. At that very moment, a wasting disease called *rattakkhamāraka* (the "red-eyed killer") manifests and kills them.
That *yakkha* devours those who are already dead and free from fear. Even those people who do not see that *yakkha*, but who fall ill from it, perceive him;
they too are seized by that disease. Thus, through the fear of this relatively recent *yakkha* and the disease, the population of the country became sparse.
59. Having heard that report, the king, while exercising his sovereignty, considered it unseemly for such fear to arise among the people;

therefore, on that very day, having observed the eightfold precepts and recollecting the ten wholesome courses of action he habitually practiced, he addressed that rākṣasa, saying, "I shall be a conqueror by Dhamma."
Resolving with even greater firmness, "I shall not rise," he lay down in the inner chamber.
By the power of his virtuous conduct and the majesty of the king, that rākṣasa was tormented;

terrified and unable to remain for even a moment, he went through the air, but at the time of the powerful dawn, being unable to enter the inner chamber, he stood outside and revealed himself to the king.
He revealed himself. When asked by the king, “Who are you? he replied: “I am a rākṣasa named Rattakkha, dwelling in a land of wicked people.
Unable to remain still for even a moment, I have been brought here, bound as if by your majesty’s power. O King, I am afraid at the sight of you.
Then the king rose from his bed, opened the lion-window, and looked out, exclaiming: “Ah! You wretch!”
“Why [do you say] ‘the man who has entered your domain’? Because he has eaten [me]. “Great King, not even a single person has been killed and eaten by me within your domain.
Rather, I eat a corpse that has become the common food for dogs, jackals, and the like; there is no offense on my part.
If there is [an offense], let the royal punishment be inflicted upon me. Having said this, while trembling, [he remained] in a state of stillness.
Unable to remain still, his hair standing on end from the force of fear, he spoke with great entreaty:
"Your Majesty’s kingdom is secure, abundant in wealth and grain, and filled with prosperity; the people are satisfied by the rain of Your Majesty’s bounty.
Even now, there are no longer many beggars. Yet, having reached such a kingdom, I have found no food for my search and my desires remain unfulfilled."
“Since I have been living in a state of wretchedness like one who is parched with thirst, I have come upon such fear as this;
O Great King, grant me safety! 61.
Then the king, hearing his piteous words, his heart trembling with compassion, said: “Do not fear, Rakkhasa!”
“I grant you safety; I give you whatever you desire,” he said.
Hearing the sound of the king and the rākṣasa conversing with one another in this way, the attendants who were inside surrounded the king.
Then, amidst their talk, the rākṣasa heard that [the king] had arrived and was conversing with him, and so all the ministers, the citizens, and the army—
Having assembled and filled both the royal courtyard and the royal palace, they raised a great clamor as the sun was rising.
Then, seeing the fourfold army assembled and the force of many thousands of warriors with weapons in hand, the Rākṣasa Sora was overcome with extreme fear;
by the power of the king’s command, he was unable to stand his ground, to move, or even to utter a word.
Seeing him in that state, the king said, "Since you have received assurance of safety, tell me what you desire.
Knowing that the righteous king would not cause him any fear, he spoke to the king alone: "Your Majesty already knows how all beings subsist on food;
for instance, O King, the inhabitants of the upper worlds live sustained by the consumption of ambrosia (*sudhā*)."
Now, the *nāgas* dwelling in this world live satisfied by eating frogs, while humans live nourished by various kinds of food such as snacks and the like.
But we, the *yakkhas*, *rakkhasas*, and others, are content with the consumption of flesh and blood.
Among them, one [of us] saw that Great Being, who was devoted to compassion, hungry and thirsty.
"Even having seen [this], my desires remain unfulfilled; being of little fortune, I grieve," he said. 63.
He spoke of his thinness, saying, "I dwell having eaten corpses. "This is true, O Great King! A dead body is as sapless as a dry leaf.
Why do you take pleasure in this wretched livelihood? Grant me a boon, O King! "Nine..."
“A man established in his domain, let one province be given to me as my pasture-ground;

there, having eaten the blood and flesh of living men while they are still breathing and their life-force has not yet departed, I shall be able to live happily for a long time,” he said. Then the king replied, “O you who are free from sin!
O Rakkhasa! I will not permit the taking of life; let go of this desire to seize [people]. “In that case,” [he said].
"Day by day, bring one human sacrifice. When he replied, "I will not give even a single living sacrifice," [the king said], "If this is true, then even the Mandisāna trees will grow without leaves;
alas, I am ruined! What shall I do? With his eyes cast down, his face darkened, overcome with dejection, and unable to offer a rebuttal, he stood there in despair.
64. Then, as compassion arose more intensely in the mind of that lord of men, it caused his heart to become agitated with a sense of renunciation. Thereupon the king reflected thus:
"Alas, I do not recall ever having let down the luster of my countenance by the heat of distress or the frustration of desires for those who came to me seeking a boon."
The faces of those who are like lotuses have become shorn of their beauty by the harsh winds of the winter season.
(66) It is never possible for this protector to cause suffering to others, and as for myself, I am [his] internal...
"I have long desired, 'When shall I give alms? Now that very time has arrived. I alone am the master of my own body;
with my own flesh and blood, I shall satisfy this [monk]. Having made this firm resolve, he summoned his ministers and spoke thus:
"This body, red and dear to me..."
I hold only to the welfare of the world;
if today I should fall into deceit,
what dear thing remains for me beyond this?

The ministers spoke thus: "For the sake of protecting one man, it is wrong to leave the entire world without a protector; what kind of path of righteousness is this for Your Majesty? Then the king spoke thus:
"I am not able to see a petitioner and yet fail to give him wealth, even if that wealth were eternal."
"Know that such a thing as this cannot be obtained even by propitiating the deities;
depart, you ministers, and do not create an obstacle to my giving," he said. Then the ministers, [realizing] that this was his firm resolve—
They said, "Let each one of us provide a portion that cannot be spared as a sacrificial offering for your protection day by day.
Then the king thought, "I myself, while still living, shall know this through various means," and he gave orders: "Bring a surgeon here quickly!
Then all the people who had gathered there, having heard that news and being devoted to his virtues, trembled with grief.
Established in that state of aversion, being exceedingly enraged, they spoke thus to one another: "Some said, 'This is a Rākṣasa;
he deserves to have his head cut off. Others said, 'His great body, resembling a dark cloud, deserves to be reduced to a mere target for hundreds of arrows.
[Others said,] 'He deserves to be struck by many hundreds of spears.'"
Others say it is fit to bring him to the state of being a target; another says, "He is to be executed by the sword-play";
others say, "Having wrapped him in oil-soaked cloth and set him ablaze with a great fire, he is to be burned. The king sanctions all of this.
Having seized this wicked man alive, having bound him with ropes in the manner of wrapping a ball of sugar, [he is to be placed] in the prison.

While others were discussing in many ways how he was to be cast in, the *yakkha*, hearing that most cruel method of execution, stood motionless as if his body were paralyzed with fear. Then the king said:
"Come, friend *rakkhasa*! You who have performed a great service!"
There is that which is to be given, there is the act of giving, and there is the mind [intent on it];
you, O blood and flesh, desire [these things].
May this difficult-to-attain union come to pass for our welfare.
"May the heart's desire of both of us be fulfilled," he said.

Having spoken thus, he addressed the *yakkha*: "Out of favor toward me, please accept this living flesh and blood being given from my own body. Then, for the sake of cutting the flesh, he extended his right arm toward the butcher’s knife.
Thereupon, that *yakkha* covered both ears and cried out: "Peace! Evil is averted; misfortune is warded off; may there be safety for the King!"
"Let it be; what has befallen me through the great ripening of my evil karma?

May the food mixed with poison live for one who desires death! Just as a forest fire surrounds one who is exhausted by the heat, if such a thought of mine should reach the Great King, then surely let the royal punishment fall upon my head;
even if the World-Protectors were to cut off my head, I would not speak thus."
“I shall not commit such an offense,” he did not accept [the king’s offer].
Then the king said, “In that case, O Yakkha! What must be done by me for you?
Thereupon, that Rakkhasa, terrified and agitated by the prospect of the slaughter of the great multitude and by the king’s command, said, “O King! I do not desire this; rather—”
"From this day forth, I desire to receive offerings and sacrifices in every village with food fit for a king," he said.
Then the king, saying, "Let the inhabitants of the realm do so," had the drum beaten throughout the city and the entire kingdom;
having exhorted them to abstain from taking life, he dismissed that yakkha.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, "The Guarding of the Night.
Now, at one time, due to the negligence of certain deities who had exceeded their allotted lifespan, a drought appeared.
By the force of the summer heat, the sun blazed fiercely.
Oppressed by heat, they drank the water everywhere;
and the fire-god and Varuṇa, afflicted by old age,
drank the cool waters of the earth.
The ripening of the unwholesome is like a garden filled with snakes;
it is like a row of forest trees scorched by the intense heat of the sun.
The sky, heated by his majesty, appears as if filled with smoke even during the rainy season for those who possess heroic power.
Covered with white clouds, it shone intensely,
as if smeared with sandalwood paste. (77) Thus,
by the great expansion of summer heat, the sands and mud remaining in the rivers, ponds, pools, and other bodies of water were dried up.

When the king heard that news—that the fields were parched, the soil in many places was cracked, and the beasts and birds were suffering from the lack of water—he felt his heart tremble with compassion.
Having undertaken the eightfold precepts, he went to the courtyard of the Mahācetiya and made this aspiration:
"May the rain fall everywhere until the entire island of Laṅkā is saturated by these streams of water. And so he caused the rain to fall.
"Even if a great flood of water should not carry me away, I shall not rise even while dying," he resolved with even greater firmness and lay down there upon a stone slab.

At that moment, by the majestic power (*dhammateja*) of the king, the gods, *nāgas*, and *yakṣas* were struck with awe; yet, through their devotion to his lineage of virtues, they became tranquil. And so, by their supernatural power (*ānubhāva*), rain-bearing clouds arose on every side. Thus it happened.
Spreading their rays in all directions like long,
unending paths, the crests of the flames expand the darkness like black clouds casting shadows over mountains.
Clouds, rumbling with deep and steady sounds,
began to rain here and there; meanwhile,
the peacocks raised their crests and let out their cries.
As they strove with supreme effort,
drops were released by them like clusters of pearls;
the streams flowed down and the dust was laid to rest.
A beautiful fragrance spread across the earth,
wafted by the wind from the clouds;
it pervaded with the splendors of Jambūnada gold.
In every direction the rainbows triumphed;
accompanied by the music of the rumbling clouds,
streaks of lightning performed as if they were dancing.
Copper-colored as if stained by anger,
roaring as if with the joy of victory,
they were like those seeking the summer heat.
Great floods then spread everywhere.
During such a rain, the king thought, "A great flood has arisen; it will submerge me," yet he did not even rise up.
Then the ministers installed water-drainage pipes on the terrace of the cetiya; filled to the brim with water from within, it submerged the king.
Then, having risen and performed the great festival for the cetiya, he went back to the royal palace. 85.

Then, perceiving that the king—who was ruling the kingdom without the use of the rod or the sword—possessed an exceedingly gentle mind, certain arrogant men became thieves, committing acts such as plundering villages. Having heard of this, the king captured those thieves alive.
Having had them arrested and cast into prison, he gave them gold, jewels, and other valuables in private, advising them, "Do not do such things," and then had them released.
At night, he brought corpses from the raw charnel ground and, as if suspecting them of being thieves, heated them with fire and threw them outside the city.
Having thus removed the fear of thieves, he once thought to himself:

86. "What is the use of this royal splendor? It is fitting that I should give away this kingdom—complete with its sovereign power, its treasury, its subjects, its harem, its ministers, and its chariots—as a gift to someone, and having entered the forest, undertake the precepts and achieve both physical seclusion and mental seclusion.
Thus he conceived a delight in renunciation. At that time, Goṭhābhaya also...
He gave rise to such an evil thought: "This king is righteous and skilled in virtuous conduct;
as he performs the ten kinds of wholesome deeds every day, his life-force increases and his obstructive karmas recede far away.
For that very reason, he will live for a much longer time. After his passing, when shall I obtain the kingdom? And having obtained the kingdom..."
Vaḍatara thought, "How shall I experience the pleasures of the senses, which are to be enjoyed by the young? Having quickly driven him away from here, I shall establish myself in the kingdom.

Taking a great deal of essential wealth, he departed through the northern gate, gathered together the former bandits, assembled a military force, and returned to seize the city gate. Upon hearing this news, the king...
“I have made a firm resolve: ‘I shall go forth into homelessness without giving the kingdom to anyone.
Yet, I suspect that by some divine power this has been brought about for me; my ministers are attempting to engage in battle even though they have not been permitted.
If this is so, a great suffering will come upon the vast multitude belonging to both sides because of me.”

"What is the use of this kingdom? Let the kingdom go back to him," he said. Then, without letting anyone know, taking only a water-strainer, and disguised so that he was difficult to recognize, he departed through the southern gate and set out for the country of Malaya, thinking:
"It is possible for those whose minds are always content to live anywhere."
"Where indeed are fruits, roots, and water not found?

(88). Thinking thus, he gradually proceeded until he entered a vast wilderness named Hatthavanagalla, which was filled with various *panasa*, mango, and *kapittha* trees, their broad branches covered with dense sprouts, flowers, and fruit.

It was crowded with various groups of trees such as *timbaru*, *jambira*, *jambu*, *vibhītaka*, *āmalaka*, *bharīta*, *katirīṭaka*, *sāla*, *sarala*, *vakula*, *punnāga*, *nāga*, *kandamba*, *āsoka*, *nīpa*, *campaka*, *bhintāla*, *tāla*, and others;
it was surrounded on all sides by vast, pure rocky peaks and reached by river junctions and bathing places; it was frequented by various herds of wild animals and flocks of birds;
it was presided over by powerful deities; and it was as lovely as the Nandana Grove.
Beholding that great forest, delightful for its easy availability of roots, fruits, and water and pleasant for its comfortable enjoyment, he thought, "This is worthy to be my penance grove.

Having established his dwelling there, through the attainment of physical seclusion and mental seclusion, with a one-pointed mind, he made his abode while devoting himself to the dwelling in loving-kindness; his body was suffused and expanded by the spreading contentment born of his other mode of livelihood.
Thus ends the seventh section, the Chapter on the Great Renunciation.
89. After King Goṭhābhaya had obtained the kingdom, after a few days had passed, he became apprehensive, thinking: "Because of my own cruelty, the circle of my kinsmen has turned its mind against me;
perhaps Saṅghabodhi, having been brought back, might at some point venture to rule the kingdom."
Intending to have him killed, he caused a drum to be beaten in the city, proclaiming: "A reward of one thousand [pieces] shall be given to whoever brings the head of King Saṅghabodhi.

Then, a certain poor man from the country of Malayadesa, carrying a meal in a leaf-wrapped bundle for his own sustenance, was traveling by way of the forest; at the time of his meal, he arrived near Soṇḍi.
Seeing King Saṅghabodhi seated there, his heart was filled with faith at the sight of the king’s dignified bearing, and he invited him for a meal;
however, the king did not accept it. He said: "I am born of a low caste, a fisherman by birth who lives by the slaughter of living beings, like a hunter;
how could I [dine] in a lineage of such supreme beauty that is worthy of such enjoyments?"
"I have been born! This food belonging to me is now being eaten by one who is auspicious and righteous"—thus he begged him again and again.
Then the king, having provided a dwelling for Chāyā with a bed, clothing, and a skin, said:
"The trees provide me with a seat from their leaf-bowls."
"Thus, for one who has acquired wealth, there is no craving for the property of others;
nor does any reproach regarding your birth and so forth exist for me.
Having said this, he did not desire anything at all.
92. Then that man, not wishing to lie down on the ground, entreated him with persistence.
Unable to resist his importunity, [the Bodhisatta] respectfully and courteously partook of the food being served and the water purified by his own strainer.
Having washed his hands and face and finished his meal, he thought: "I am now another; what kind of benefit can I do for him?"
Thinking, "I shall do him a service in return," he brought the man before him and asked, "What is the news in Anurādhapura?
Then that man said, "Having driven out the former king, a king named Goṭhābhaya has established himself in the kingdom;
and in the city, a reward of one thousand [pieces of gold] is being offered for whoever brings the head of King Sirisaṅghabodhi."
"He has had a drum beaten, it is said, that he may hear [my fame].
Immediately upon his words, with a heart thrilled and exultant, [I thought]:

"Now, by this gift of my thousandfold royal head, a repayment for him will have been made; because of this internal gift, the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) will reach its ultimate limit. And furthermore—
Not even as much as a single rotten wood-apple are these heads and living skins worth;
yet my head is fit for the sake of enlightenment.
For the sake of gaining wealth for a traveler;
moreover,
it is like a grove of reeds that causes only affliction.
"Regarding this putrid body, a mere heap of bones,
which has experienced suffering even while being cared for:
may I make it fruitful by applying myself to my own true goal."
Having reflected and determined what he wished to do, he said, "O man, take my head and go;
show it to King Sirisanghabodhi. Having heard this, the man replied, "Your Majesty, we shall not contemplate such a great and sinful deed; I am afraid."
95. Then the king said, “Do not fear; for the sake of obtaining a thousand coins, I myself will provide the means for you. You must simply act according to the conditions I have set.

When the traveler, greedy for the gain of a thousand, consented, he was unable to find a sword for the execution of the decapitation; thus, by the power of his resolve in the Dhamma, his head remained attached to his body.
Thinking, "I shall give it away after setting it apart," he made his cross-legged posture firm and, preceded by a feeling of joy, made an aspiration:
"May this gift of my head be a condition for the attainment of omniscience.
Then, addressing that man who stood near him, he spoke. That superior man had never before seen, heard of, or performed such a difficult deed.
"Taking the head that has been given, go to Anurādhapura and show it, saying, 'I recognize this watchtower; he will believe me regarding the watchtower.
Then, Goṭhābhaya, if he believes him, you should act thus: 'If he believes him, I shall give a thousand [pieces of gold] with him as witness';
and you must proceed to that place in this manner. Having thus instructed her on how she should act, he said, "Come, good man..."
Having stood near the weaver, he said, "Joining your hands in *añjali* as a sign of seeking both goals,
extend your arm," and having thus properly positioned the bamboo tube by making the blue lotus stalks on both sides straight,
he moistened the joint at the head with water along the line of the mark, using his own right [hand].
Firmly grasping the hair tied in a topknot with his clenched fist, he made this resolution:
"Until I have taken my plough and handed it into the hand of the traveler, let the movement of my mind and the force of the wind-element continue without interruption.
Having resolved thus, he lifted the topknot upward. At that very moment, the knot on his head became loosened and spread out; by that [action], the right...
Even as he was still grasping it with his fist, he placed the traveler’s hand upon the dripping stream of blood;
at that very moment, the deity presiding over the forest, her voice resonant with cries of "Excellent!", caused a rain of flowers to fall and took charge of the protection of the head.
In this mire of the night of worldly existence, within the field of the hands of the Buddhas,
where the supreme seed of the head has been sown and from which it has sprung forth—
the creeper of the perfection consisting of giving belonging to this [Bodhisattva]—
May the fruit-flavor of omniscience delight the people. 97.

Then that traveler, having adorned the head with garlands of fragrant forest flowers, placed it in a basket, and traveling with swift speed, arrived at Anurādhapura and presented it to Goṭhābhaya; upon seeing it, he—
Being unable to produce [the head] and having fallen into doubt, he stood there.
Then the traveler, recollecting the instructions given by the King, took that head, threw it into the air, and with palms joined in reverence, looking up toward the sky, he entreated: "O Lord!
Great King Sirisaṅghabodhi! May you be my witness in this matter. Then that head, possessed by a deity, remained suspended in the supportless space.
Having gained a foothold in the sky and facing Goṭhābhaya, he thought:
"I am this very Sirisaṅghabodhi, the king’s well-wisher;
my heart is fulfilled by the manner in which I have offered my head."
"And you, O King, shall obtain the glory and happiness of sovereignty;
let this very attainment of a thousandfold [wealth] be yours as you proceed," he said. 99.
Having heard that, Goṭhābhaya, along with his ministers, with a heart full of fear, prepared the lion-throne and raised the white parasol over it.
Having had [the body] brought here, O King, he requested permission to descend; having descended there, he honored that head with various kinds of offerings, paid homage, and asked for forgiveness.
Having performed the funeral rites with great magnificence, he satisfied Aṅika with a thousand kahāpaṇas and sent him away.
Thus ends the eighth section: the Internal Gifts.
100. But Sirisaṅghabodhi, the king’s chief queen, having learned of the king’s flight, thought, “I too shall follow him.
Disguised in another form, she departed through the southern gate; not knowing the way, she abandoned the direct path and entered various villages.
Seeing no sign of her husband, and being both terrified and unable to endure hunger, she—
Thinking, "He has surely gone to the country of Malaya," she traveled by way of Vaṅka; unable to go quickly due to her delicate nature, she delayed for some time.

Then, having heard news of the king's distribution of gifts in a village near that forest region, her heart was filled with grief as she thought, "I, wretched as I am, did not obtain even a mere sight of him.
Thus, with a heart overflowing with sorrow, she ascended into that very grove of trees.
Searching for her husband’s body, she questioned the crowds of people in the nearby villages;

wandering here and there because she did not know the sign of his cremation, the children, cowherds, wood-gatherers, and women living in those neighboring villages heard her lamentation and, their hearts trembling, accompanied her as she wandered. Thus, like a female osprey, she [searched] upon the earth.
Seeing a forest grove with its blossoming flowers and stainless sands, she fell there and, rolling about on the ground, uttered most piteous lamentations;
even today that place is designated by the name "The Widow’s Place.
Having spent that entire night right there in great weeping, on the following day she wandered here and there.
And wandering about, burning with a great fire of grief and unable to endure their torment, they fell into a certain small pool of water;
having plunged in and remained submerged for two or three moments due to the force of their fainting, they regained consciousness and extinguished their feverish heat.
Consequently, that place has since received the name "The Nibbāna Lotus Pond."
102. Then, having risen, she searched the ground, the trees, and the rocks;
and near a cave, she saw a withered trunk-like body lying there, unharmed by jackals or other predators due to the intervention of a deity.
With her heart bursting from the force of her grief, she embraced that corpse more tightly and lay down; for such was the wretchedness caused by her arrival there.
There, from the impact of her body falling down, she died at the very same moment as the swoon, her complexion turning dark blue.
103. The inhabitants of the nearby village gathered together and said, "It is not fitting for people like us to touch the bodies of the anointed king and the chief queen;
nor is it proper for us to perform the funeral rites without first informing the reigning king."
Considering it improper [to remain], they built a hut to ward off the heat of the rainy season and constructed a fence to prevent the entry of wild animals, and then departed. 104.
Goṭhābhaya, recollecting the series of virtues of King Sirisaṅghabodhi that were not shared by any other, [proceeded].
From his childhood onwards, his constant devotion to the three refuges as his sole resort, his perpetual guarding of virtue, his lack of doubt regarding the teachings of the Sugata,
his mastery of all arts and sciences, his lack of interest in kingship, his generosity, and his performance of difficult deeds such as the subduing of the Rākṣasa—
how could these not bring joy to that conscious being, especially when he was a traveler in distress?
For the sake of gaining a thousand [pieces of gold], he personally extracted his own head from its neck and offered it as a gift;
that this head remained suspended in the supportless sky, and that this announcement was made with a voice so distinct and full of intent— this is a marvel and a wonder, never heard before,
and a stainless conduct that does not even coexist with the stain of my great transgression.
"It will continue for a long time; alas, I shall be censured by the virtuous with such ill-repute that endures so long—
especially since I have usurped the kingdom and caused the execution of such a great being,
a noble personage who was always my true friend, solely through an act of treachery against a friend."
Thinking, “I shall be entangled,” he was overcome by fear and trembling even as he emerged from the water;
shaking with agitation, he approached [the king], wondering how he might release this great sinner.
Then, it occurred to him that in order to perform the punishment for that offense, a noble and superior wholesome deed (*kusalakamma*) ought to be done.
Then, having assembled his ministers and deliberated with them, he reached a decision; instructed in the same manner by the Great Saṅgha,
he set out with a vast army, established a camp not far from that forest region,
and [arrived at] the field of merit which was a witness to the difficult deeds of that Great Being.
Having gone there in person to the vicinity of the distillery and observed a suitable spot,

he displayed his royal majesty by having the cremation ground adorned like a city of the gods; then, having had a funeral pyre constructed higher than usual out of exclusively large quantities of sandalwood,
he had it fashioned with Jambūnada gold— equal in weight and proportion to the King’s head, including the neck.
Having had a tube fashioned in the shape of a head by shell-workers and joined it to the form of a torso, they had a golden crown resplendent with various jewels placed upon it;
having likewise adorned the Great Sage, they clothed both of them in costly *dukūla* fabrics similar to those used in Kāśī,
placed them upon a golden couch inlaid with many gems, and [anointed them] with sandalwood...
Having placed [the body] upon the funeral pyre and kindled the fire with pure fuel,
surrounded by many young kṣatriyas, he himself stood there and, having sprinkled it with hundreds of jars of ghee,
held a great festival for the cremation ground. On the very next day, after extinguishing the funeral pyre with a great multitude of people, he erected a cetiya at that spot.
Thinking that it would be appropriate to construct the palace in a circular shape, he summoned his ministers and said:
"At present, the construction of a multi-storied, exceedingly vast, golden circular palace cannot proceed due to the lack of those capable of protecting it;
furthermore, even the plasterers of the kingdom are stealing the gold out of greed for it. Therefore, [build one] made of non-metal, suitable for easy maintenance, and of appropriate proportions."

Having deliberated that it was appropriate to construct both the circular hall and the cetiya before long, he mobilized a great military force and, according to the aforementioned instructions, had a two-storied circular mansion built.

Inside it, he had a reliquary containing the relics of the Sugata and a venerable cetiya constructed. On a day of great festivity, he showed these to the Great Saṅgha and said, "This, Venerable Sirs..."
In former times, the Great King Sirisaṅghabodhi reigned over the land of Laṅkā under a single umbrella; now,
I have had a two-storied circular vimāna constructed like an umbrella above the umbrella for that king’s memorial image,
and having joined a golden pinnacle to the top of the cetiya like a crown, [I have done so] with the approval of all gods and men.

Having said, "I have been made to fall into a state of humiliation like that of a lowly candāla," he entrusted to him many village lands belonging to the Cetiya monastery and more than a thousand attendants;
and at the foot of the mountain, he established various monasteries for the Saṅgha, complete with hundreds of palaces,
monastic cells, walkways, places for night-quarters, day-quarters, Dhamma halls, gate-towers, walls, and other such structures.

Having had it constructed and having granted numerous villages and fields together with their inhabitants for the constant provision of requisites to the community of many thousands of monks dwelling there, he declared:

"This Mahāvihāra, which stands like a raised banner over the Mahālekharaṭṭha kingdom, is the family treasure of the Kṣatriya lords who are the masters of the land of Laṅkā; it must be protected by all Kṣatriyas."
Having instructed the kṣatriya princes in the midst of the great multitude, saying, "Prosperity must not be squandered;
it must be constantly protected," he went to the city of Anurādhapura. Furthermore, in order to dispel that evil karma, he performed great meritorious deeds in various monasteries.
From that time forth, by the kṣatriyas who had attained sovereignty over Laṅkā...
Furthermore, that Great Vihāra of Hatthavana-galla was periodically restored by Mahāmaccā and others, and it continued to function without any decline in its maintenance.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, "The Arising of the Circular Mansion."
107. Then, on another occasion, while residing in a certain monastery among a great community of monks,
some elder monks, being forest-dwellers (*āraññaka*), sat down in a certain place within the monastery and, applying themselves to meditation,
increased their insight (*vipassanā*) and attained *arahantship*, filling the sky with the roar of their great attainment.
108. At that time, while King Upatissa was ruling the kingdom, he heard that terrifying sound of the earth during the middle watch of the night.
Thinking, "What will happen to me?", he was unable to find sleep due to his distress and was consumed by grief.
Then a deity, adorned with white parasols and garments, said to him: "Do not fear, Great King! There is no ill omen from this cause."

When it was said, "In the Hatthavanagalla Mahāvihāra, certain great elders attained Arahatship," he asked what the reason for the earth quaking at the time of that elder’s attainment of Arahatship was;
he was reassured that this was the fruit of a wish he had made in the past while performing meritorious deeds, when he prayed:
"May I become an Arahant after making the earth resound along with the sky."

109. Having heard this, the king—his heart filled with faith because that elder’s victory over the defilements was even more distinguished than that of the remaining bhikkhus who had attained arahantship—paid homage to the Great Elder.

He then thought, "I shall honor the spot of ground that served as the seat for his festival of the destruction of the taints by constructing a palace there," and taking a great army with him, he went to that place.
Having gone to that place, she had a great five-storied palace constructed;
having had it adorned with various kinds of paintings and covered with floors inlaid with gold and copper, she decorated it like a celestial mansion.
Having settled the Great Elder, whose taints were exhausted, there together with the community of monks, she attended upon him and his retinue with the four requisites.
Having established villages and fields near his palace, he departed.
Then, after the lapse of a long time, certain bandits living in the Malaya region banded together and carried out a plundering of the villages;
being intoxicated by the great acquisition of wealth, they gave money and raised an army, and for the most part became masters.
Having offered sacrifices on a grand scale, they plundered the great monasteries, seized the golden-tiled roofs, and having destroyed the great palaces,
they caused them to fall. At that time, King Moggallāna, while ruling his kingdom, heard of this occurrence and went into their presence.
Having observed them, he caused them to divide one another by means of gifts, honors, and dissensions;
as those thieves were thus divided, they fought with one another and became weak on their own accord.

Then the king, knowing them to be disunited, took his own army, went there, and having captured them individually, he beat the drum of safety throughout the kingdom and established the countryside in peace.
Having had those abandoned dwellings restored to their original state, they fell the Great Palace at the time of collecting gold.
Hearing of this, [the King] realized, "Just as in the past it was covered with gold plates, so too will such misfortune arise hereafter.
Thus, having had it built with three stories and constructed the palace as before, he had it covered with layers of clay.
Having restored the circular palace and having had all the monastic dwellings returned to their original state, he departed.
Thus ends the tenth chapter, "The Origin of the Palace.
112. Then, among the many [beings] who were ornaments to Laṅkā, whose vast power of merit and psychic prowess was manifest, and who were like the very embodiments of the Triple Gem—

When the lords of Laṅkā had become mere remnants of their former fame and merit, having strayed from the path of righteousness and being devoid of the proper measures required for the protection of the kingdom;
and when even the ministers and attendants had grown weak and were for the most part living in mutual opposition;

then, due to some past and cruel evil karma of the inhabitants of Laṅkā, there entered [the island] those dwelling in various regions who were ignorant of the Teacher’s doctrine and seized by the grasp of false views.
The enemy armies, having arrived here from Jambudīpa, rendered the entire island of Laṅkā agitated by manifold calamities.
At that time, being most severely oppressed by that enemy army, the king, the royal ministers, and others, along with many thousands of people,
their hearts trembling with fear and seeking protection, fled from village, town, and city to various difficult and inaccessible places.
Having lived there with great difficulty, those of great effort— guardians of the relic of the Sugata’s tooth who were exceedingly diligent—
then took two tooth-relics and two excellent bowl-relics and proceeded to a difficult-to-enter region called Kunnamalaya,
a mountain pass; yet even there, being unable to protect them, they buried them in the ground and departed as they pleased.

114. Prior to that, there was a king named Vijayabāhu, an intimate confidant of the righteous King Dhammāsoka—the ornament of the Solar dynasty and sovereign of the entire Jambudīpa—who had sent princes of the same lineage as himself along with Jayamahābodhimiṇḍa;
this king was the legitimate son of King Vijayamalla, whose succession had been transmitted through a line of descendants including grandsons and great-grandsons.
Having established the excellent city named Jambudvīpa— a path of noble policy practiced by the virtuous, endowed with a perfected army and transport— and residing there,
he caused the victory over all adversaries to be achieved by his great military force; then, from the regions of Kuntala and Malaya, he had the Blessed One’s tooth-relic, the venerable lord,
and the supreme relic of his bowl brought forth, [placing them] in a most resplendent casket resembling a celestial chariot.
Having constructed a celestial mansion (*vimāna*) and enshrined that pair of relics within it, he served them with great reverence through extensive offerings.

While generating a vast field of merit for the Blessed One’s eighty-four thousand sections of the Dhamma, he—along with King Dhammasoka (Dhammika) and King Sirisanghabodhi—established a most enchanting site, purified by the dust from the feet of many thousands of *khīṇāsava* (those whose taints are destroyed), who were like the very essence of the Kshatriya caste. There, by the Great King Goṭhābhaya...
Formerly, when a host of heretics led by King Rāḷa of Cōḷa— having arrived during a time of national calamity—

shattered the Great Cetiya at its core as if it were their own life-force, and the Blessed Relics had vanished, [the king] seized the golden railings and other ornaments from near the heart-base (hadayavatthu) and,

through the process of pouring streams of molten lead, caused [the damage] to be restored. This was done in the circular temple that serves as an ornament for the Hatthavanagalla Mahāvihāra, which he had commissioned.
Restraining himself from the very moment he began the offering of flowers, he had a great golden pinnacle and a pair of *abhaya* (fear-dispelling) statues fashioned with care;
having bestowed villages, fields, and other lands along with their inhabitants,
and having established a continuous cycle of regular almsgiving for the monks residing there, he made that Hatthavanagalla Mahāvihāra prosperous in every respect.
115. Now, when that lord of Laṅkā had become nothing but a remnant of his fame, his son, the king named Parakkamabhuja, [commemorated] from the time our Blessed One,
the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, defeated the host of Māra,
and attained the sovereignty of perfect enlightenment, for one thousand eight hundred and twenty-four years.
And when several years had passed, having attained the consecration of sovereignty, he—
having won over the great masses of people through various means of conciliation and having constantly gratified the Saṅgha of many thousands of monks with gifts of the four requisites—

[offered] a casket of jewels resplendent with many gems and red jewels, shaken from the pride of enemy royal families by the strength of his own arms, along with a golden casket worth five thousand pieces of gold.
Having commissioned a silver casket for the tooth-relic of the Blessed One using twenty-five thousand measures of silver,
with a heart of exceeding faith, he sent a fine rain of gold there; and having caused his own city and the Temple of the Tooth Relic to be thoroughly adorned,
he took the supreme relic of the ten powers with great reverence and [offered] many [gifts] to the Blessed One.
Having recollected the accounts of the past deeds of conduct of former kings, who were inspired by the display of miracles,
his pair of ears was now satiated as if by the nectar of the stories thus circulating; thinking, "By some special miracle,
my recovery of sight must also be made fruitful," he performed an act of propitiation with great reverence.
116. At that moment, that tooth-relic performed a miracle, displaying the grace of a royal swan upon the palm of his hand.

How so? Just as the Bodhisatta, in his final existence, immediately upon being born from his mother’s womb—descending from the swaddling cloth brought by the hands of the best of men—though still a child, appeared like one sixteen years of age; and though unadorned, appeared as if adorned with many garments and ornaments.
Even though he was walking upon the ground, he appeared to all people as if he were traveling through the sky;

likewise, at that time, the venerable Tooth Relic, manifesting its form with its beautiful image, auspicious marks, and limbs, scattering many kinds of rays of light, made itself known to the people gathered there. For it is said:
“O royal swan upon the lotus-hand of the Lord of Laṅkā,
having fashioned those ten relics into the form of the Supreme Sage,
she shines brilliantly with many spreading rays of light.”
And all the cardinal and intermediate directions were beautifully adorned.
Seeing that most wonderful marvel, his heart was filled with serene confidence,
like a universal monarch who has obtained the precious wheel-treasure.
The lord of men honored that peerless relic with many excellent ornaments of jewels and other precious objects. Then,
at the time of his profound faith in the supreme tooth-relic of the Jina, the great warrior-king Parakkamabāhu— possessing majesty through his splendor, power, and valor— [acted].
The exceedingly audacious one, who resided in Pulatthipura; who had brought about the destruction of the world’s dispensation; who, together with the king, led a Colan army numbering many thousands;

whose prowess was like that of a rutting elephant or a lion before numerous regional lords; who was difficult to overcome; who had filled the entire world by means of gathering the world’s dispensation;
who possessed abundant forces and vehicles; and who had come from the region of Tambaliṅga desiring to seize the sovereignty of Laṅkā—[he was subdued].
Having brought King Vaṇḍabhānu, along with his vassal princes, into his presence, and having made the entire island of Laṅkā subject to a single umbrella [of his sovereignty],

he performed the gathering of the world’s religious teachings at double the scale of his own great king. Once, desiring to provide the *kaṭhina* robes for the Saṅgha, he had all the necessary preparations—
such as the processing and spinning of cotton— completed in a single day, and [offered] many precious items individually.
Having caused to be given eighty sets of *kaṭhina* robes, adorned with precious jewels and complete with the requisites for monks and novices,
he filled the ten directions with the world’s acclaim.
Thus, accomplishing many other such meritorious deeds that inspired wonder in the world, that great hero, King Parakkamabāhu—
Having had a Great Cetiya constructed at the cremation site of his own paternal grandfather in the Hatthavanagalla Vihāra,
and having heard that a magnificent palace— once inhabited by many thousands of *khīṇāsavas*— had remained abandoned there for a long time,
he dispatched a preeminent minister named Patirājadeva, born of the Dhanukhetaka royal lineage and endowed with the excellence of faith and other virtues, and through him...
Having caused a palace to be built— beloved in the city, adorned with three stories, and filled with jasmine flowers— at a cost of many thousands of dhanas,
he established a regular provision of requisites for the many monks dwelling therein.
In that very place, having placed rafters on the lower floor of the circular mansion, he constructed a covering all around.

Having had a two-storied mansion constructed, he then built a three-storied one; desiring to have a temple for the Victor (Jinamandira) built there on the island of Laṅkā such as had never existed before,
he first dug a pit measuring one man’s height at the northern side of the circular mansion,
removed the earth, filled it with river sand, and established a foundation adorned by a royal elephant.
From the foundation up to the pinnacle, having divided the walls and roof into eight sections, each of the eight wall-parts was adorned with various colorful patterns;

above them, the structure was decorated with numerous spirits and servants dressed in various costumes and playful ornaments that evoked the essence of sport and jest, as well as with staff-bearers and eunuchs;
it was enchanting with diverse painted figures on the front and borders, exceedingly high, covered with lattices, and finished with a coating of plaster.
Having fashioned a gateway adorned with a *makara* arch, it was brilliantly illuminated by various kinds of artistic works such as charming floral garlands and vine-patterns arranged within;
it featured well-constructed staircases, doors, and panels, and was beautified by a graceful and enchanting life-like image of the Buddha Kassapa in a decorated niche.
To the right of that image, it was further adorned with a statue of the Sugata carved from solid rock.
He had a great celestial mansion (*vimāna*) built with three stories.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the Section on the Arising of the Eight-Sided Mansion.
Or rather, [it is so called] because of the clearing away of debris or due to new construction work.
And by means of the procedure for the donation of fields and so forth, they shall also [ensure] that in the future,
those virtuous ones who maintain this monastery shall have their names inscribed here,
even if it be only a single letter.
